summary: This work presents a digital quantum simulation of three-level Jaynes-Cummings dynamics on IBM Quantum superconducting processors, encoding a qutrit in two qubits and a cavity mode in one qubit, with evolution implemented via first- and second-order Suzuki-Trotter decomposition. Comparison across IBM backends reveals a trade-off between algorithmic accuracy and hardware noise: second-order Trotter provides better excitation-number conservation and reduced population leakage, but first-order circuits achieve higher aggregate fidelity (~94.6% on ibm_marrakesh vs ~88.4% for second-order), with ibm_torino most faithfully preserving Jaynes-Cummings selection rules despite lower calibration-based fidelity.
motivation: Multi-level light-matter interactions exhibit richer coherence control and quantum interference phenomena than two-level systems, but extending Jaynes-Cummings models to three-level atoms on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware requires systematic investigation of how digital discretization errors and hardware noise compete.
method: A qutrit is encoded as two qubits with enforced selection rule $q_2 = 1 \Rightarrow q_1 = 1$, and cavity photon number in one qubit; Hamiltonian terms are decomposed via Suzuki-Trotter steps with calibrated $R_Z$ rotation angles set by the experimentally relevant coupling scale $g \approx 2\pi \times 25$ kHz and time step $\Delta t$ chosen such that $g \Delta t \lesssim 0.1$–$0.2$ rad.
result: Circuit fidelity estimated at ~90% on ibm_torino (dominant readout error 2.95%, two-qubit error 2.437 × 10$^{-3}$, single-qubit error 3.086 × 10$^{-4}$); second-order implementation shows sharper population confinement within excitation-conserving subspace despite deeper circuits, while time-dependent measurements exhibit coherent Rabi oscillations in $P_{|1\rangle}(t)$ with suppressed higher-state population $P_{|2\rangle}(t)$ remaining negligible.
